newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-AUSTRIANS SLAM SKI CHAMPIONSHIPS FAILURE.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-AUSTRIANS SLAM SKI CHAMPIONSHIPS FAILURE.

text.p: Instead of basking in glory as they had expected, Austria's Alpine skiing team has yet to win a single title and is being slammed at home as world championship failures.
But despite the heavy criticism, coaches from the ski-crazed country shrugged off the pressure on Friday.
With only one day and three races remaining in Sestriere, the highly fancied Austrians have been watching others take the main medals.
They have managed only three bronzes through veteran Guenther Mader in super-G, Mario Reiter in combined and Andreas Schifferer in giant slalom.

The biggest upset came from the men's downhill squad, a dominating force on the World Cup circuit this season. Fritz Strobl, a favourite for the blue-riband event, missed the podium by one-hundredth of a second.
"We never had high expectations, what we had, and still have, is hope," insisted men's coach Werner Margreiter. "You need a lot of luck to win a medal, so much can go wrong on one day."
Thomas Sykora, a favourite for Saturday's floodlit night slalom who has won five of the winter's eight World Cup slaloms staged so far, said: "I don't care what the media is reporting."
"I have no pressure. I will just do my best."
But the Austrian media think differently about the richest and largest team on the Alpine circuit and many are talking about an "economic disaster."
The Austrian government and numerous sponsors pump around seven million dollars a year into their ski federation, of which over four million is for the Alpine division.
The Austrian federal chamber of commerce and sponsors finance an Austria House at every Alpine skiing world championship which serves as a daily hospitality centre for Austrians and other guests.
In Sestriere, the cost of running the Austria House is estimated at around $650,000.
Peter Schroecksnadel, president of the Austrian Ski Federation, said financial difficulties were not likely before the 1998 Nagano Olympics because most sponsors had agreed to two-year contracts.
"If our performance is not better in Nagano, then we could face difficulties renewing these contracts," said Schroecksnael.

Austria ski pool general secretary Reinhold Zitz warned that one of the leading ski companies -- which signed a one year contract with World Cup slalom title-holder Elfi Eder -- could pull out of women's racing before next winter.
Austrians have seldom found success at world championships, bringing home only a single gold from Morioka in 1993 and Sierra Nevada last year.
The last time Austrians failed to take a gold at a world championships was in 1987 in Crans Montana.
But Austrian Alpine director Hans Pum saw little reason to worry and said other favourites, such as Sweden's Pernilla Wiberg and Frenchman Luc Alphand, had also not lived up to expectations.
"We were well prepared but mistakes can happen," he said. "Our athletes gave their best. They all wanted to be world champions.
"We will never blame a single one of them for not trying."
According to Pum, Austria's biggest problem in Alpine skiing was that they have too many good athletes.
"Our racers have the pressure of performing well all winter in order to make the world championship or Olympic team -- which allows only four starters per country.
"This doesn't happen in other, smaller teams," Pum said when asked why many Austrian skiers often appeared tired and lacking energy at big events.
"As long as we continue to produce so many good ski racers, there is little we can do to solve the problem," he said.
